title: Trigger Rules: When Skipped Is Not the Same as Success
description: A pipeline DAG has three tasks in sequence: `extract → validate → load`. The `validate` task produces a 'skipped' status on days when there is no new data for that partition. In most DAG-based orchestrators, `load` only starts when ALL upstream tasks succeed. What problem does this default create, and what is the correct fix?
options: No problem — 'skipped' is treated as 'success' by all modern orchestrators, so `load` runs normally when `validate` skips
The pipeline should be redesigned so `validate` never marks itself as skipped — it should return an empty result set instead, which signals success to downstream tasks
When `validate` skips, `load` stalls — 'skipped' is not 'success'. Change `load`'s trigger rule to 'all upstream completed' so success and skip both allow it to proceed
`load` should be split into two tasks: one that depends only on `extract` for no-data days, and one that depends on both `extract` and `validate` for days with new data
explanation: In DAG-based orchestrators, 'skipped' is a distinct terminal state that is not the same as 'success'. A downstream task with the default trigger rule ('all upstream must succeed') will remain blocked if any upstream task is skipped — the pipeline stalls for that run without error. The canonical fix is to change the trigger rule to 'all upstream completed' (also called 'all done'), which treats success, skip, and failure as all satisfying the completion condition. This is a standard pattern for conditional or data-availability-dependent DAGs. Option A is wrong — modern orchestrators (Airflow, Dagster, Prefect) distinguish skipped from success precisely to support conditional branching. Option B avoids the root issue — marking a task as skipped is an intentional signal that a conditional branch was not taken; returning an empty result forces downstream tasks to run even when there is genuinely nothing to load. Option D adds structural complexity where a configuration change is the designed solution.
hints: A 'skipped' task communicates something different from a 'succeeded' task — it says 'this branch was intentionally not taken', not 'the work is done'. Does your downstream task's trigger rule account for that distinction?

Orchestrators let you configure when a task becomes eligible to run. If the default waits for all upstream tasks to succeed, which trigger rule would you use to also allow skips as a valid completion state?

title: SLA Breach: When 'Close Enough' Is Not Enough
description: A daily pipeline ingests sales data and has an SLA: complete within 45 minutes of its 6:00 AM scheduled start — i.e., finish by 6:45 AM — so analysts have fresh data before their 7:00 AM standup. On Monday, the pipeline ran for 52 minutes, finishing at 6:52 AM. An analyst says: 'The data was ready 8 minutes before the standup — no SLA breach.' A data engineer disagrees. Who is right?
options: The data engineer is right — the SLA deadline is 6:45 AM; finishing at 6:52 AM is a 7-minute breach, regardless of downstream impact on this run
The analyst is right — no downstream user was impacted, the report was ready before 7:00 AM, and SLA compliance should be interpreted in terms of actual business impact
The analyst is right — SLA compliance is measured over a rolling 30-day window; a single run that exceeds the threshold is a minor deviation, not a formal breach
Neither — the 6:45 AM deadline is a target, not a hard limit; SLAs always carry an implicit tolerance band unless explicitly stated otherwise
explanation: An SLA is a defined operational commitment — 'finish by 6:45 AM' means exactly that. Running for 52 minutes and finishing at 6:52 AM is a 7-minute breach, regardless of whether downstream users noticed or were impacted on this occasion. The analyst conflates two distinct things: (1) the SLA definition (a time-bound commitment) and (2) the business impact of this specific breach (happened to be minor). SLA tracking matters precisely because the threshold exists to ensure reliable downstream systems at scale — if this pipeline consistently runs 50–55 minutes, every run breaches the SLA, and eventually a user will arrive at 6:51 AM for an early call and find stale data. Option B is wrong because business impact is the motivation for an SLA, not its definition. Option C is wrong because SLA compliance is per-run against the defined threshold, not a rolling average — a 30-day average is a separate reporting metric. Option D invents a tolerance band that is not part of the stated SLA.
hints: The SLA says the pipeline must finish by 6:45 AM. It finished at 6:52 AM. Does the fact that no analyst was harmed on this run change whether the defined deadline was met?

SLAs exist to enforce reliability at scale, not just to protect a specific downstream user on a specific day. What would happen if 'no one noticed, so it doesn't count' were a valid interpretation every time the pipeline ran slightly over?

title: Batch vs Streaming: Latency vs Throughput
description: An operations team must decide between a batch pipeline (runs every hour) and a streaming pipeline (processes events within seconds) for updating a customer-facing 'order status' dashboard. Orders are placed throughout the day and customers expect near-real-time status updates. Which approach is appropriate and why?
options: Batch — hourly aggregates are sufficient for dashboards; streaming is only needed for fraud detection
Streaming — customers expect near-real-time status; an hourly batch pipeline introduces up to 59 minutes of lag between an order update and its reflection on the dashboard
Batch with 5-minute intervals — this provides low enough latency without the operational complexity of streaming
Streaming is never preferable to batch because streaming systems are inherently less reliable due to out-of-order events
explanation: Latency is the deciding factor. If customers expect status updates within seconds, an hourly batch job can leave them waiting up to 59 minutes for their order to move from 'processing' to 'shipped' — an unacceptable user experience. Streaming (or micro-batch) pipelines are designed for exactly this low-latency requirement. Option A incorrectly limits streaming to fraud detection. Option C is a reasonable middle ground but 5-minute polling is still batch and introduces unnecessary scheduling complexity compared to event-driven streaming. Option D is wrong — streaming systems are mature and production-proven; out-of-order handling is a solved problem with watermarks and event-time semantics.
hints: What is the maximum acceptable lag between an event happening and it appearing in the dashboard? Match that to the pipeline frequency.
Batch is simpler to operate but has bounded-by-schedule latency. Streaming has near-zero latency but adds complexity.

title: Delivery Semantics Under Consumer Restart
scenario_context: A Kafka consumer processes payment events and writes results to a relational database. The consumer commits offsets after each successful database write. During a deployment, the consumer process crashes after writing a record to the database but before committing the offset to Kafka.
description: What is the delivery semantic of this system, and what is the consequence of the crash?
options: Exactly-once — the idempotent write to the database ensures no duplicates regardless of offset commit timing
At-most-once — because the consumer crashed before committing, the event is permanently lost
At-least-once — uncommitted offset causes re-read on restart, risking a duplicate write if the write is not idempotent
Exactly-once — Kafka guarantees exactly-once delivery to any downstream system when transactional producers are enabled
explanation: Committing the offset after a successful write is the at-least-once pattern: if the process dies after writing but before committing, it restarts and re-reads the uncommitted offset, processing the event again. This guarantees no events are lost but risks duplicates if writes are not idempotent. At-most-once would commit the offset before the write (so a crash after commit but before write loses the event). Exactly-once across Kafka and an external relational DB requires an atomic transaction spanning both systems — Kafka transactions alone do not achieve this. Option A is partially right (idempotent writes prevent duplicate rows) but incorrectly labels the semantic as exactly-once when the system design is at-least-once. Option B inverts the semantics. Option D overstates Kafka's transactional guarantee scope.
hints: Trace what happens on restart: which offset does the consumer resume from, and does it re-process any events?
At-least-once = commit after write (risk: duplicates on restart). At-most-once = commit before write (risk: loss on crash).

title: Diagnosing Growing Consumer Lag
scenario_context: A Kafka consumer group processing a high-volume clickstream topic has been running stably for two weeks. This morning, consumer lag on the topic began growing steadily. No deployments or configuration changes occurred. CPU and memory on consumer nodes are at 40% utilisation.
description: What is the most likely root cause, and what is the correct first diagnostic step?
options: The consumer is under-provisioned — add more consumer instances immediately since lag means the consumer is at capacity
Kafka broker disk is full — growing lag is always caused by broker-side I/O bottlenecks
The consumer group rebalanced and one partition is now unassigned — check for unassigned partitions in the consumer group status
A producer-side spike is the most likely cause — check whether the topic's incoming message rate increased (e.g., traffic spike, upstream retry storm) before scaling consumers
explanation: Growing lag with low resource utilisation suggests the producer is writing faster than usual, not that consumers are too slow. A traffic spike, upstream retry storm, or a new producer sending to the same topic would all increase the rate and cause lag to grow even if consumers are nominally healthy. The correct diagnostic order is: (1) check producer throughput trend on the topic, (2) check consumer throughput, (3) check partition assignment. Scaling consumers first without diagnosing can lead to a consumer-side overload if the spike subsides. Option A jumps to scaling without diagnosis. Option B is implausible with 40% disk utilisation. Option C is a valid secondary check but unassigned partitions would show as zero consumption on that partition, not uniform growing lag.
hints: Low consumer resource utilisation with growing lag points to the producer side — check whether the incoming rate changed.
Diagnose before scaling: understand whether the problem is consumer capacity, producer volume, or partition assignment.

title: Small-File Problem: Root Cause and Fix
scenario_context: A Spark pipeline writes Parquet files partitioned by `event_date` and `event_type` to S3. After three months, the S3 prefix contains 2 million files averaging 50 KB each. Downstream Athena queries on date ranges are extremely slow due to excessive listing and open operations.
description: What is the root cause of the small-file problem and what is the most effective fix?
options: The file format is wrong — switch from Parquet to ORC, which automatically compacts small files during writes
High partition cardinality — (event_date × event_type) creates many combinations each receiving few records. Reduce granularity and run periodic compaction
Increase Spark executor memory — small files are created when executors run out of memory and flush early
The S3 consistency model causes small files — switch to a consistent object store like HDFS to fix the listing performance
explanation: Small files arise when partitioning cardinality × write frequency creates many combinations, each receiving few records per write cycle. With daily writes and many event types, each (date, type) partition may only receive a handful of records per run — producing tiny files. The fix is twofold: (a) reduce partition granularity (e.g., partition by date only, filter by type at query time), and (b) schedule a periodic compaction job that reads existing small files and rewrites each partition as a smaller number of larger files. Option A is wrong — ORC does not auto-compact. Option C misattributes small files to memory pressure. Option D is wrong — S3 strong consistency is already the standard since 2020, and small files are a data engineering concern unrelated to consistency semantics.
hints: High-cardinality partitioning + frequent small writes = many tiny files. The fix is either coarser partitioning or periodic compaction.
A compaction job reads small files per partition and rewrites them as a few larger files — it's a standard maintenance pattern for Parquet on object stores.

title: Schema Evolution Under Backward Compatibility
scenario_context: A data engineering team maintains a Kafka topic with an Avro schema registered in a schema registry under BACKWARD compatibility mode. The current schema has fields: user_id (string), event_ts (long), amount (double). A producer team wants to add a required field checkout_channel (string, no default) to capture a new business attribute.
description: Can the schema change proceed as described? If not, what is the correct approach?
options: No — a required field with no default breaks BACKWARD compatibility: old messages lack the value and cannot be deserialised. Add a default (e.g., null)
Yes — adding a new field in BACKWARD mode is always safe because consumers receive all fields
No — any schema change under BACKWARD mode requires a major version bump in the registry and a consumer-side upgrade before the producer can write new messages
Yes — the schema registry will automatically infer a null default for new fields under BACKWARD mode, so no explicit default is needed
explanation: BACKWARD compatibility means a newer schema can read data written with an older schema. If a new required field has no default, a consumer using the new schema cannot deserialise old messages (which were written before the field existed) — they have no value to populate the new field. The fix is to add the field as optional with a default (e.g., `null` for a nullable union, or `'unknown'` for a string with default). FORWARD compatibility would cover the reverse direction (old consumer reading new messages). Option B is wrong — consumers using the new schema cannot fill in a required field from old records. Option C misrepresents schema registry mechanics — versioning is automatic and a major bump is not required for backward-compatible changes. Option D is wrong — Avro does not auto-infer defaults; the default must be explicitly declared in the schema.
hints: BACKWARD compatibility = new schema can read old data. Ask: can a consumer with the new schema deserialise a message written with the old schema?
A new required field (no default) breaks BACKWARD compatibility — old messages have no value for it. Add a default to make it safe.

title: Diagnosing a Silent Lineage Failure
scenario_context: An analyst reports that the 'daily active users' metric in the BI dashboard dropped 30% last Tuesday but recovered the next day. No pipeline failures were logged. A data engineer investigates and finds the raw event log on S3 has correct row counts for Tuesday, the Spark job that processes it completed successfully with no errors, and the downstream metrics table shows the anomaly.
description: Given that the pipeline succeeded and raw data is intact, what is the most likely silent failure category and the correct investigation approach?
options: A silent failure — dropped rows from a join mismatch, over-restrictive filter, or skipped partition. Audit per-stage counts
Network partition between S3 and the Spark cluster caused partial reads — check CloudTrail for S3 GetObject errors on Tuesday
The BI tool is caching stale data — clear the BI cache for Tuesday's date range and the metric will correct itself
Tuesday's data was a genuine traffic anomaly — a 30% drop is within normal variance for daily active user counts
explanation: A successful job status with intact raw data that produces anomalous output is the hallmark of a silent data quality failure. Common causes: (1) a join that produces fewer rows than expected due to a key type mismatch or upstream schema change; (2) a filter that was overly restrictive on that day's data; (3) a partition being silently skipped because an upstream partition was empty or mis-dated. The investigation approach is row-count auditing at each stage: raw → after join → after filter → output table. A drop at a specific stage locates the failure. Option B is unlikely given S3 and Spark both reported success. Option C conflates BI caching with pipeline data quality. Option D dismisses a 30% anomaly without investigation — that is never the correct first response.
hints: When raw data is intact and the job succeeded but output is wrong, the failure is inside the pipeline logic — compare row counts stage by stage.
Silent drops often happen at joins (key type mismatch) or filters (a column's distribution changed and the filter became over-restrictive).

title: Partition Pruning Trade-Off Under SLA
scenario_context: A petabyte-scale data lake stores events partitioned by `event_date`. A new reporting requirement asks for a rolling 90-day window of events, re-aggregated every hour. The current job scans all 90 partitions on each hourly run. Query execution takes 45 minutes end-to-end. The SLA is 60 minutes.
description: The job currently meets the SLA, but the team is asked to design a more efficient approach. Which strategy best balances correctness, efficiency, and SLA headroom?
options: Run the job only once per day at midnight — 90-day rollups don't change materially within a single day
Increase cluster size by 10× — the current approach is correct and scaling compute is simpler than redesigning the pipeline
Switch the partitioning from event_date to event_hour — this lets the job scan exactly 90×24 = 2160 partitions more precisely
Incrementally process only the new partition (today's data) each hour and maintain a pre-aggregated 90-day summary table that is updated with an upsert — read 1 partition per run instead of 90
explanation: The incremental + summary table pattern (also called a 'lambda-lite' or 'incremental materialization' approach) is the standard solution for bounded-window aggregates that are refreshed frequently. Instead of re-scanning 90 partitions each run, read only today's new partition and upsert the result into a pre-built summary. The 89-day history is already aggregated in the summary. This reduces each hourly run from 45 minutes to seconds while maintaining correctness as long as the summary is partitioned and upserted correctly. Option A violates the 'hourly update' requirement. Option B works but is expensive and provides no long-term scalability as the window grows. Option C increases partition count 24×, adding overhead rather than reducing it.
hints: For a rolling window that is refreshed frequently, ask: does each run need to re-read the full history, or can incremental updates to a summary table replace most of the scan?
An incremental + summary table pattern reads only new data per run and merges it with pre-aggregated history — reducing scan cost by orders of magnitude.
